title: Police cleared in death of man in custody near Toronto airport
article: The province's civilian police watchdog has cleared Peel regional police after a man died in custody near Pearson International Airport.
The Special Investigations Unit says police responded to a 911 call July 24 after 53-year-old Keith Prescod allegedly struggled with a GO Transit bus driver for control of the vehicle on Dixon Road.
Police restrained Mr. Prescod after he had left the bus and struggled with an airport employee.
He lost consciousness and was pronounced dead at Etobicoke General Hospital.
SIU director Ian Scott says that after an autopsy it appears Mr. Prescod's death was the result of a pre-existing medical condition exacerbated by the ingestion of cocaine and physical exertion.
Mr. Scott says the legal cause and manner of death will be determined by an inquest.

Animosity between police in Ontario and the civilian agency that oversees them is at an all-time high, the province's Ombudsman said as he released a report that portrays officers as far more interested in protecting their own instead of the public.

But the government comes in for the harshest criticism for failing to bring in laws that would give the Special Investigations Unit more power in doing its job. As a result of this failure, officers did not co-operate in nearly one in three cases investigated by the SIU between October, 2008, and October, 2011, undermining the public's confidence in the police watchdog, Ombudsman André Marin says in a report released on Wednesday.

The report, titled "Oversight Undermined," criticizes the Ministry of the Attorney General for not introducing legislation that would prevent lawyers from vetting police officers' notes from incidents under investigation by the agency. The practice can compromise an investigation because officers can too easily be tempted to refashion their recollections if they have received advice from a lawyer, the report said.

The ministry is also doing nothing to stop an officer under investigation and the officers who witnessed the event from being represented by the same lawyer, the report says. This practice makes it difficult for the SIU to have confidence that the accounts obtained from witness officers are based on independent recollection and not tailored to match the evidence of others or to protect a fellow officer.
"The animosity between the SIU and the police is palpable and at an all-time high. I think police are running roughshod over the SIU," Mr. Marin said at a news conference.

This is Mr. Marin's second report on the SIU. In the latest one, he trains his sights on the ministry, accusing officials of "systematically" discouraging the director of the SIU from speaking out about the problems and suppressing an annual report prepared by the agency that documented problems with police.
The SIU investigates when police are involved in an incident that causes serious injury or death. During fiscal 2010, it investigated 33 cases involving deaths.
One of the cases highlights how the ministry is "actively" undermining the SIU, the report says.

Ruth Schaeffer, who attended the news conference at which the report was released, told reporters her 30-year-old son, Levi, was schizophrenic and wanted to live in northern Ontario far from distractions. Mr. Schaeffer cycled from Peterborough to a remote campsite on Osnaburgh Lake in June, 2009. He was alone when two Ontario Provincial Police officers who were investigating the theft of a boat began questioning him.
Mr. Schaeffer was shot and killed when he approached one of the officers armed with a knife and refused to obey commands to stop, the Ombudsman's report says.

The SIU did not lay criminal charges against the officer. However, in his report to the Attorney General, which is quoted in Mr. Marin's report, SIU director Ian Scott said he had no "information base" that would have indicated if charges were appropriate, because the police officers refused to provide the SIU with the draft version of their notes.

The officers prepared their notes two days after the shooting and only after they had consulted with their lawyer, who also represented 10 witness officers who became involved in the case after the shooting. The first draft of their notes remains in the custody of their lawyer. The only version the SIU saw was the one approved by the lawyer.
"[The officer]never has to tell me what happened," said Ms. Schaeffer, who was at the Ombudsman's news conference. "I will never know the circumstances of my son's death."
Attorney General John Gerretsen acknowledged that change is needed, but was noncommittal. "The situation needs to be improved," he told reporters. "We're going to improve it."

Mr. Marin said he is skeptical the ministry will follow through on his call for legislation. He cites an internal briefing note from the Attorney General's office dated March 30, 2009, suggesting the government had no intention of pursuing legislative reform in response to his 2008 report.
"He usually gets his media hit off report releases and then moves on," the note says of Mr. Marin, who is renowned for garnering widespread media attention.
